title: PBM Adjudication Rejection Volume Metric
scenario: A digital pharmacy is tracking prescription submissions through PBM adjudication. The operations team wants to measure how many claims are being rejected to identify periods when manual intervention spikes.
prompt: The operations manager proposes tracking 'Total Rejected Claims' as the key metric to understand adjudication load. The team reviews this metric weekly in their ops standup to decide when to hire additional pharmacists for claim resolution. What is wrong with this metric as proposed?
instructions: One short sentence: name the flaw, propose a fix.
stakeholder_rationale: Shows us the absolute workload our care team must handle each week for rejected claims.
reference_answer: Should be normalized per script submitted. Rejection Rate (rejected claims / total claims submitted) is better.

grading_rubric.description: Answer states the metric is not normalized (per script, per claim submitted, or per 1000 scripts)
Answer recommends a rate metric with both numerator and denominator (Rejection Rate, % rejected, rejected per submitted)
Answer states or implies total volume scales with submission volume and obscures true rejection frequency

hints: Consider what happens if the pharmacy doubles its script volume next month.
Think about whether this metric lets you compare rejection frequency across different time periods.
What mathematical transformation would make this metric robust to changes in total submission volume?
common_mistakes: Proposing to segment by rejection reason without fixing the normalization issue
Suggesting median instead of mean (not relevant here since we need a rate, not a central tendency)
Recommending a per-pharmacist metric when the core flaw is lack of per-script normalization

metric_movers.reason: Population size changed (e.g., script submission volume doubled after a large employer group launched)
metric_movers.explanation: Total rejected claims will rise with submission volume even if rejection rate stays constant.

metric_movers.reason: Per-script rejection likelihood changed (e.g., PBM tightened PA requirements for specialty drugs)
metric_movers.explanation: Tighter PA rules increase the rejection rate, driving more total rejections independent of volume.

metric_movers.reason: Script mix shifted toward higher-rejection categories (e.g., more specialty vs retail fills)
metric_movers.explanation: Specialty scripts reject at 25-40% vs 10-15% for retail; mix shift raises total rejections even at stable per-category rates.

metric_movers.reason: Measurement definition changed (e.g., team started counting refill-too-soon as rejections when they previously didn't)
metric_movers.explanation: Expanding what counts as a rejection inflates the total without reflecting operational reality change.

metric_movers.reason: External event increased script demand (e.g., flu season drove refill volume surge)
metric_movers.explanation: Seasonal demand spikes submission volume, mechanically raising total rejections even if rejection rate is flat.

metric_movers.reason: Auto-recycling logic improved (e.g., formulary substitution flow now auto-resolves 20% of rejections)
metric_movers.explanation: Fewer rejections reach the manual queue, lowering total rejections and the manual workload.

metric_movers.reason: Patient app UI redesigned (e.g., new onboarding flow for first-time users)
metric_movers.explanation: Onboarding changes do not affect PBM adjudication logic or rejection likelihood for submitted claims.

metric_movers.reason: Telehealth visit completion rate improved (e.g., provider no-show rate dropped)
metric_movers.explanation: Visit completion is upstream of prescription submission and does not directly move claim rejection counts.
